analysis.one_liner: Speeds cheaper generic drugs to market and lets pharmacies import prescription drugs from Canada.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill 78-21 to speed cheaper generic drugs to market and allow prescription drug imports from Canada, but the House never voted on it before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill attacked two of the main reasons prescription drugs cost so much. First, it rewrote the rules for generic drugs: brand-name companies would have to register their patents with the FDA on time or lose the right to sue over them, could no longer trigger an automatic 30-month delay of generic approval with patents filed late, and could not sit on or trade away a first generic competitor's 180-day head start. Second, it let licensed pharmacists and wholesalers import U.S.-made prescription drugs from Canada, where they sell for less, with testing and record-keeping safeguards. It also gave states temporary federal money for Medicaid and allowed states to negotiate Medicaid-style drug rebates for residents not on Medicaid. The Senate passed it 78-21. The House never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers — especially senior citizens and the uninsured — would gain from faster generic competition; CBO estimated generics save purchasers $8-10 billion a year and cost 25-60% less than brand-name drugs. Importation from Canada would add a second path to lower prices. State governments would gain temporary federal Medicaid funding and new authority to negotiate drug rebates for uninsured residents. Generic drug makers would gain faster approval paths and clearer rules.

how_it_helps.text: CBO estimated that substituting generics for brand-name drugs could save purchasers $8-10 billion a year, with generics costing 25-60% less — an average of $15-30 per prescription.

It limits the 30-month automatic freeze on generic approval to patents properly filed with the FDA, and bars brand-name companies that never sue within 45 days from suing later — closing a route used to delay generic competition.

It takes away the first generic applicant's 180-day exclusive marketing right if that company stalls — failing to market, withdrawing its application, or settling with the brand-name maker — so a generic that wins its patent challenge actually reaches pharmacy shelves.

It lets licensed pharmacists and wholesalers import U.S.-made prescription drugs from Canada, where prices are lower, with testing and record-keeping safeguards, and directs regulators to tolerate clearly personal-use imports of up to a 90-day supply.

It clarifies that states can negotiate Medicaid-style drug rebates for residents not on Medicaid, and provides temporary federal money to states, including $3 billion in block grants and a modest increase in the federal Medicaid match.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose revenue from shorter monopoly periods, fewer delay tactics, and Canadian price competition. The federal treasury would bear the cost of the temporary state fiscal relief. The FDA and HHS would take on new testing, registration, and enforcement work for importation.

drawbacks.text: Title II was designed to take effect only if the Secretary of Health and Human Services certified that it posed no additional public health risk and would significantly cut consumer costs — a self-imposed condition so demanding that it could have prevented the importation provisions from ever operating.

Importing drugs across borders carries a real risk of counterfeit or substandard products reaching patients; the bill responded with batch testing, detailed chain-of-custody records, registration of Canadian sellers, and authority to suspend imports, but the risk is inherent to the policy.

The bill bars courts from considering a generic applicant's ability to pay damages when deciding whether to grant an injunction, and requires generic applicants' proposed formulation and method-of-use information to be kept confidential — provisions that favor generic companies in patent litigation.
The bill appropriated $3 billion in emergency-designated federal funds for state fiscal relief and temporarily increased the federal Medicaid match, adding to federal spending.
Requiring patents to be registered within 30 days or losing the right to sue for infringement is a harsh penalty that could forfeit legitimate patent rights over a paperwork lapse.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were large and concrete: CBO estimated $8-10 billion a year in savings from wider generic use, generics cost 25-60% less than brand-name drugs, and the bill closed specific legal routes that kept generics off the market while opening a legal channel for cheaper Canadian imports. The costs are real but smaller: added federal spending for state fiscal relief, new safety-regulation burdens on importers, a litigation framework tilted somewhat toward generic applicants, and a genuine counterfeit-drug risk the importation title tried (with testing, records, and suspension authority) to manage. The importation section's self-certification requirement was a serious design weakness that could have kept it from ever operating. On balance, the bill would likely have lowered drug prices for ordinary Americans at a cost mainly to brand-name manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 78-21, but the House received it in September 2002, held it at the desk without referring it to committee, and never voted on it before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Schumer on May 1, 2001, but the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee did not report it until July 11, 2002 — more than a year later.
On July 17, 2002 the Senate voted 99-0 to end debate on taking up the bill, and then agreed to consider it.
The Senate debated the bill across two weeks in July 2002, and a cloture motion (a vote to end debate and move to a final vote) was filed on July 29.
On July 31, 2002 the Senate invoked cloture 66-33; every one of the 33 votes against ending debate came from Republicans.
Later that day the Senate passed the amended bill 78-21, with all 50 Democrats and 28 of 49 Republicans in favor.
The Senate sent the bill to the House on September 4, 2002, where it was received and held at the desk; no further action was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the patent-based delays and pricing the bill would have curtailed, and House leaders avoided a politically difficult vote on drug prices.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate passed the bill 78-21 with all 50 Democrats and 28 of 49 Republicans in favor, but all 33 senators who voted to block a final vote were Republicans, and the Republican-led House never brought the bill up.

industries.note: The bill shortens the periods during which brand-name companies can keep generics off the market: late-filed or unregistered patents can no longer trigger a 30-month approval freeze, companies that don't sue within 45 days lose the right to sue at all, and settlements that park a first generic's exclusivity trigger forfeiture. Allowing pharmacists to import cheaper U.S.-made drugs from Canada adds further price pressure. Every one of these provisions works against revenue built on extended patent-protected pricing.

Generic companies would reach market sooner through faster approval paths, limits on 30-month stays, and clearer claim-by-claim patent certifications. The bill also cuts both ways for them: forfeiture rules strip their 180-day exclusivity if they sit on it, and litigation provisions on injunctions and confidential formulation information tilt in their favor.

Licensed pharmacists and wholesalers gain a legal channel to import U.S.-made prescription drugs from Canada, subject to registration, testing, and record-keeping requirements — potentially letting them buy at Canadian prices and pass some savings to customers.

States would get temporary fiscal relief: a 1.35 percentage-point increase in the federal Medicaid match for fiscal 2002-2003, a $3 billion block grant for social services through fiscal 2004, and explicit authority to negotiate Medicaid-style rebates with drug makers on behalf of residents not enrolled in Medicaid.
